topic: The Great Bridge: Connecting Slopes and Areas (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus)
target_audience: Senior high school or first-year university students

sections.title: The Runner's Puzzle: A Tale of Two Tasks
sections.content: Introduce a scenario involving 'Zippy the Cheetah' to illustrate two different problems: 1) Finding speed from position (Differentiation) and 2) Finding distance from speed (Integration). This sets the stage for the inverse relationship.
sections.example: Visual: Zippy runs across the screen. Graph A shows his position over time; Graph B shows his velocity. We ask: 'If we have the graph of his speed, how do we find the total distance he covered?'

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: Slopes and Sums
sections.content: Briefly recap the derivative as the 'slope of the tangent' (rate of change) and the definite integral as the 'area under the curve' (accumulation). Use motion graphics to show a tangent line sliding along a curve vs. color filling the space beneath it.
sections.example: For the function f(x) = x², show the slope at x=2 is 4, while the area under the curve from 0 to 2 is a specific shaded region.

sections.title: Accumulation: Building the Area Function
sections.content: Explain the concept of an 'Area Function' A(x). Instead of a fixed area, imagine a vertical slider moving along the x-axis, accumulating area as it goes. This introduces the idea that area itself is a function of the endpoint.
sections.example: Animation: A vertical 'scrubber' moves from x=0 to x=5. As it moves, the shaded area grows, and a new graph (the Area Function) is plotted simultaneously above it.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem: The 'Undo' Button
sections.content: Reveal the core of the FTC: The rate at which the area accumulates is exactly equal to the height of the original function. Therefore, the derivative of the integral is the original function. This establishes the inverse relationship.
sections.example: Formula Visualization: d/dx [ ∫ f(t) dt ] = f(x). Show a 'Math Machine' where you drop in a function, it gets integrated into an area, then differentiated back into its original shape.

sections.title: Application: The Antiderivative Shortcut
sections.content: Demonstrate the practical use of the theorem: To find the area under f(x), we just need to find its 'Antiderivative' F(x). Explain the Evaluation Part: ∫[a,b] f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a).
sections.example: Back to Zippy: If Zippy's speed is v(t) = 2t, the area (distance) is found by the antiderivative t². To find distance from t=0 to t=3, calculate 3² - 0² = 9 meters.

sections.title: Summary: The Beautiful Symmetry
sections.content: Consolidate the lesson. Emphasize that differentiation (breaking down into slopes) and integration (building up into areas) are two sides of the same coin. This symmetry is why we call it the 'Fundamental' theorem.
sections.example: A split-screen visual: On the left, a curve being 'sliced' into slopes; on the right, the same slices being 'stacked' back into the original curve's area.
